name: Google App Engine
summary: Google’s original platform as a service: describe your app in an `app.yaml`, run one deploy command, and Google runs and scales the instances.
intro: An App Engine app belongs to one Google Cloud project and holds one or more services. Each `gcloud app deploy` creates a new version of a service, and each version runs on as many instances as its traffic needs. You can move all traffic to a version, split traffic between versions, or reach any version directly at its own URL, which makes rollbacks and canary tests a routing change rather than a redeploy.

There are two environments. The standard environment runs your code in a sandbox on a Google-maintained runtime for Go, Java, Node.js, PHP, Python or Ruby. Instances start in seconds, a service can scale to zero, and you pay per instance hour after a daily free allowance. The flexible environment runs your app as a Docker container on Compute Engine VMs: any language, background processes, WebSockets and SSH, but instances take minutes to start, at least one is always running, and you pay for vCPU, memory and disk.

Google now steers new work elsewhere. Its documentation calls Cloud Run “a newer and better alternative to App Engine” and recommends Cloud Run to new Google Cloud users. Cloud Run runs on much of the same infrastructure as the standard environment, and Google publishes a guide for migrating to it.
strengths: The standard environment scales to zero and has a daily free tier: 28 instance hours of the F classes and 9 of the B classes, then $0.05 an hour for the smallest class
Versions and traffic splitting are built in, so you can deploy with `--no-promote`, test the version at its own URL, then shift traffic
Deploys and instance starts take seconds in the standard environment, and Google patches the runtime in place
Services in one app act like microservices that share the project’s other Google Cloud resources
limits: Google recommends Cloud Run instead for new projects, and each standard runtime has end-of-support, deprecation and decommission dates you must upgrade around
The standard sandbox only lets you write to `/tmp` and has no background processes, WebSockets or SSH; automatically scaled requests time out after 10 minutes
The flexible environment never scales below one instance, takes minutes to start and deploy, has no free tier, and its VMs may be restarted weekly for patching
Projects created after March 2025 cap standard services at 20 instances by default unless you raise `max_instances`

story: In 2008 putting a web app online meant renting servers and setting up load balancing, scaling and a database yourself. On April 7, 2008, at an event called Campfire One, Google launched a preview of App Engine, which let developers run web apps on Google’s own infrastructure. Product manager Paul McDonald described the goal as making it easy to start a new web app and then easy to scale it to millions of users. The preview offered automatic scaling and load balancing, a datastore built on Bigtable and GFS, and Google APIs for sign-in and email, for the first 10,000 developers who signed up.

The first version was strict. Apps had to be written in Python, could not write to the filesystem, could only run in response to a web request, and had to respond within a few seconds. Those rules let Google spread requests over many servers and start and stop them freely. App Engine left preview on November 7, 2011, three and a half years after Campfire One, with more than 300,000 active apps and a 99.95% SLA for paid apps on its High Replication Datastore.

Many apps needed more than the sandbox allowed, so Google added a second environment that runs Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs; it reached general availability in March 2017 with the pitch “Any language. Any framework. Any library.” In April 2019 Google announced Cloud Run, which runs any container and scales to zero. Google now describes Cloud Run as building on more than a decade of running App Engine and recommends it to new users.

choices.choice: A sandbox instead of a server
choices.why: Limiting what an app could do (no local writes, no subprocesses, short requests) let App Engine route any request to any server and start or stop servers to match traffic, without the app noticing.

The 2008 preview gave every app 500 MB of storage, 200 million megacycles of CPU a day and 10 GB of bandwidth a day, which Google estimated at about 5 million page views a month, and promised those quotas would stay free. The team summed up its philosophy as “easy to use, easy to scale, and free to get started.”

The flexible environment accepted any Docker image, so developers could bring languages the standard runtimes lacked, and the same container could also run on Google Container Engine, Compute Engine or their own servers.

timeline.text: Preview launches at Campfire One: Python only, for the first 10,000 developers
Leaves preview with release 1.6.0 and a 99.95% SLA for paid apps
Flexible environment, running Docker containers on Compute Engine VMs, becomes generally available
Google announces Cloud Run and second-generation App Engine runtimes
New projects get a default limit of 20 instances per standard service
